references.text: The Mosaic law on inheritance: When a father divides his property among his sons, the firstborn shall receive a double share. In [ref:5 Mos 21:16-17|Deuteronomy 21:16-17], the principles of inheritance are established that form the background for the younger son's claim to his portion of the estate.

In [ref:Ordsp 29:15|Proverbs 29:15] it is warned that a young man left to himself brings shame upon his mother. The younger son's demand for inheritance while his father is still alive reflects this kind of foolishness and self-will.

[ref:Ordsp 20:21|Proverbs 20:21] says that an inheritance quickly gained at the beginning will not be blessed in the end. The younger son who demands his share early is an illustration of this principle.

The next verse, [ref:Luk 15:13|Luke 15:13], tells what happened after the father divided the property: the younger son gathered all he had and went to a distant country, where he squandered his wealth in reckless living.

In [ref:Luk 15:31|Luke 15:31] the father says to the older son: "All that I have is yours." This shows that after the younger son received his share, the rest of the father's estate belonged to the eldest—the father's division in verse 12 had lasting consequences.

[ref:Sal 16:5-6|Psalm 16:5-6] speaks of the Lord as one's portion and inheritance. The younger son's demand for his share of the earthly inheritance stands in contrast to those who have the Lord as their portion and inheritance.

[ref:4 Mos 27:8-11|Numbers 27:8-11] gives laws concerning inheritance distribution in Israel. These rules form the legal background for the younger son's claim to receive his share of his father's property.

In [ref:Luk 12:13|Luke 12:13] a man asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide the inheritance with him. This situation recalls the younger son demanding his share of the inheritance and shows an obsession with material wealth.
